title: Gout
path: Management of Clients with Musculoskeletal Problems

headings.title: What is Gout?
headings.content: Gout is a very painful type of inflammatory arthritis that happens when uric acid crystals build up inside the joints. It usually starts suddenly, often attacking the big toe, leaving the joint hot, swollen, and so tender that even the weight of a bedsheet causes severe pain. While the big toe is the classic spot, gout can also strike the ankles, knees, wrists, and fingers. The attacks come and go in waves, with symptom-free periods in between, but if left untreated, these flare-ups become more frequent and can damage the joints permanently.

headings.title: How Uric Acid Causes Gout
headings.content: Uric acid is a normal waste product that forms when the body breaks down chemicals called purines. Purines are found naturally in your body and also in certain foods and drinks like red meat, seafood, and beer. Normally, uric acid dissolves in your blood, passes through your kidneys, and leaves the body in your urine. However, when the body produces too much uric acid or the kidneys fail to filter it out fast enough, a condition called **hyperuricemia** develops. Over time, this excess uric acid turns into sharp, needle-like monosodium urate crystals that settle in and around the joints.

headings.title: Risk Factors and Triggers
headings.content:
Not everyone with high uric acid develops gout, but certain factors greatly increase your chances. 

- **Diet**: Eating a diet rich in purines, especially red meat, shellfish, and drinking alcohol like beer, raises your risk.
- **Weight**: Carrying excess weight makes the body produce more uric acid, and makes it harder for the kidneys to clear it.
- **Medical conditions**: High blood pressure, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and poor kidney function are closely linked to gout.
- **Genetics**: A family history of gout makes you more vulnerable.
- **Gender and age**: Men develop gout more often and at a younger age than women, though women's risk catches up after menopause.

headings.title: Signs and Symptoms
headings.content:
A gout attack usually starts very quickly, often overnight, and reaches its worst pain within twelve to twenty-four hours. 

- **Intense joint pain**: The affected joint hurts severely, even when resting.
- **Lingering discomfort**: After the sharp pain subsides, mild joint discomfort can last from a few days to a few weeks.
- **Inflammation and redness**: The skin over the joint becomes bright red, purplish, swollen, and feels hot to the touch.
- **Limited movement**: As swelling increases, you will find it hard to move the joint normally.

headings.title: Medical Diagnosis
headings.content: Doctors use a combination of physical exams, patient history, and specific tests to confirm gout. Blood tests measure uric acid levels in the blood, though a person can have gout and still have normal uric acid levels during an acute attack. The most definitive test is joint aspiration, where a doctor uses a small needle to withdraw fluid from the inflamed joint. Looking at this fluid under a special microscope reveals needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals. X-rays may also be used, not to diagnose early gout, but to rule out other joint problems or check for long-term joint damage.

headings.title: Medical and Pharmacological Management
headings.content: Treating gout involves two main goals: managing painful acute flare-ups and lowering uric acid levels to prevent future attacks. During a flare, medications like **NSAIDs** (such as ibuprofen or indomethacin), **colchicine**, or **corticosteroids** are used to quickly reduce pain and severe inflammation. Once the acute attack settles, doctors prescribe long-term urate-lowering therapy, such as **allopurinol**, to reduce uric acid production and stop crystals from forming. It is important to know that starting a uric acid-lowering drug can sometimes trigger a temporary flare, so doctors often prescribe a short-term anti-inflammatory drug alongside it.

headings.title: Nursing Care and Patient Education
headings.content: Nurses play a key role in helping patients manage gout and prevent future painful episodes. During an acute attack, the nurse should handle the affected joint with extreme care, elevate the limb, and apply cool compresses if tolerated to soothe inflammation. Educating the patient is vital for long-term success. Nurses must teach patients to drink plenty of water to help flush out uric acid, limit alcohol and purine-rich foods, and take their prescribed medications exactly as ordered—even when they feel completely well.
